title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within‑task experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) to test whether embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) loop increases detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated network configurations and improves bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation. Using a synthetic intent→configuration suite (N=270 tasks; 3 vendor syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks), gpt-5-mini as generator, and a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet deterministic validator/emulator as ground truth, we observed no verifier rejections: baseline accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded (verify → optional bounded repair) accepted 270/270 (100%); bounded repair was never invoked. Paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], exact McNemar two‑sided p=1.0; bootstrap resamples=10,000, seed=1729). The preregistered generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation=false), i.e., the same single generated candidate was evaluated under both arms; this design choice is the proximate cause of the degenerate outcome and is stated and analyzed explicitly. All preregistration, execution traces, validator/scoring JSONs, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 hashes are released (see execution/*; preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0; master prompt archived provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). We interpret this artifact‑backed null result in light of generation semantics, task difficulty, verifier design, and bounded repair budget and outline reproducible next steps.

sections.introduction: Motivation. Natural‑language intent→configuration pipelines driven by large language models (LLMs) promise to simplify NetOps but introduce operational risk: stochastic LLM output may be syntactically plausible yet semantically unsafe on devices. A pragmatic safety architecture is Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR): generate a candidate configuration, use a deterministic verifier (oracle) to accept/reject against formal rules, and when rejected invoke a bounded repair loop that uses verifier diagnostics to produce corrected candidates. Research question and conditional scope. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment asking: does embedding a deterministic verifier as an oracle inside a bounded GVR loop (max 1 repair attempt per rejected candidate) increase detection/rejection of unsafe/incorrect LLM‑generated configurations and improve bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation? Crucially, the preregistered design used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) so the same single generated candidate per task was evaluated in both arms. We therefore frame the contribution precisely: an artifact‑backed measurement of the verifier’s marginal effect conditional on an identical generated candidate per task.
sections.related_work: Positioning. Our architecture follows the Generate–Verify–Repair framing used for safe AI code generation and other regulated domains [doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899]. We build on deterministic/formal network verification work (e.g., NetKAT/weighted NetKAT decision procedures for network safety reasoning [doi:10.1145/3808318]) and on recent LLM→intent‑translation and intent‑based NetOps studies that propose LLM‑centric IBN pipelines and verifier‑anchored agentic systems [openalex:W4400072049, openalex:W4386722061]. Unlike broad LLM benchmark papers, our contribution is an artifact‑anchored, preregistered execution that records every model call, validator trace, and SHA‑256 artifact hash to permit deterministic reproduction and audit.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design freeze. The full experiment plan was preregistered (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; preregistration JSON SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Paired design: N=270 distinct intent→configuration tasks (3 vendor syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks). Validation subset: preregistered 20% stratified sample (54 tasks) reserved for verifier–emulator concordance validation.
Generation semantics (registered, decisive). The preregistered and executed generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation=false): for each task we generated a single candidate and evaluated that identical candidate under both the baseline and guarded arms. This choice is recorded and frozen in the preregistration and in execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 a40e96e2...). It implies model_calls_used=270 (one generation per pair) and explains why the verifier/repair pipeline would not be exercised if generated candidates were verifier‑acceptable.
Models, verifier, budget. Generator: gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). Verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implemented on Dockerized Kathará/Mininet emulator (deterministic emulator used as ground truth). Guarded arm policy: generate → verifier; if verifier rejects, invoke bounded repair loop (≤1 repair call). Baseline: evaluate same generated candidate with verifier. All provider calls, responses, and validator traces were logged, hashed, and archived (execution/*; representative scoring JSON execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 350bfaa2e...).
Metrics and analysis. Primary outcome: paired detection/rejection proportion difference. Statistical test: exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Missingness and exclusion rules were preregistered; full deterministic reconciliation and per‑artifact hashes are provided in execution/execution_manifest.json.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and provenance (artifact facts). Planned episodes: 540 (270 pairs). Completed: 540; failed: 0. Model calls used: 270 (shared_initial semantics). Representative artifacts (examples and SHA‑256): execution/model_configuration.json (a40e96e2...), execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (350bfaa2...), execution/execution_manifest.json contains the full per‑artifact manifest and hashes.
Primary empirical outcome (artifact‑backed numbers). Baseline verifier‑accepts: 270/270 = 100%. Guarded final acceptances: 270/270 = 100%. Verifier rejections of initial candidate: 0/270. Bounded repair calls invoked (guarded arm): 0. Repair successes conditional on initial reject: 0/0 (no repairs attempted). Validation subset (54 tasks) verifier–emulator concordance: 54/54 (false_accept=0, false_reject=0).
Statistical inference (preregistered analysis executed as specified). Paired contingency: n11=270, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Estimated paired difference = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples; seed=1729). All raw analysis artifacts and logs are archived (analysis/*; e.g., analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 62cd99d7...).
Interpretation of the numeric result. The observed degenerate contingency (zero discordant pairs) is an artifact‑grounded fact produced by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics together with the generator producing verifier‑acceptable candidates at the chosen settings. Therefore (A) the verifier/repair path was not exercised, and (B) the numerical p=1.0 and CI=[0.00,0.00] are degenerate and not informative about verifier utility under independent stochastic resampling. These arithmetic facts are recorded in deterministic_reconciliation and analysis artifacts.
sections.discussion:
What the results show and do not show. Show (artifact‑backed): conditional on the exact preregistered execution semantics (one shared generated candidate per task) and the chosen generator/settings, the inserted deterministic verifier produced no additional rejections and no repairs were invoked. Do not show: that verifiers are unnecessary in general, or that GVR is ineffective under different generation semantics, sampling regimes, model choices, adversarial inputs, or larger repair budgets. Why the degenerate null occurred. Two preregistered decisions jointly explain the null: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced one generated candidate per task that both arms evaluated; (2) the generator configuration and prompt led to verifier‑acceptable outputs for these synthetic tasks. Both decisions and their exact artifact traces are archived (execution/model_configuration.json; execution/responses/* and execution/scoring/*). Practical implications. Studies that aim to measure verifier/repair effectiveness should (and, if reproduced, must) vary generation semantics and sampling to create the opportunity for verifier invocation. The artifact bundle allows deterministic replication and targeted variant experiments.
Recommended reproducible follow‑ups (precise, artifact‑anchored). Each follow‑up is implementable from the provided artifacts and preregistration fields: (1) independent generation per arm: set independent_condition_generation=true in the experiment plan and rerun (this doubles model calls and enables between‑arm sampling variability); (2) increase stochasticity: vary sampling temperature and seeds to expose stochastic failure modes; (3) expand task difficulty and add adversarial/OOD intents drawn from realistic operator error modes; (4) increase bounded repair budget (allow multiple repair attempts per rejected candidate) and test repair convergence behavior; (5) test multiple generator models (other model identifiers) and multiple verifier rule‑sets (conservative vs permissive) to map verifier false‑accept/reject tradeoffs. All these parameters are controllable in the preregistration fields and the execution harness and are explicitly reproducible using the archived artifacts (execution/* and the full hash manifest).
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired experiment integrating a deterministic network verifier into an LLM GVR pipeline. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the chosen generator/settings, the single generated candidate per task was verifier‑acceptable for every one of N=270 tasks; verifier rejects and bounded repairs did not occur, producing a measured paired difference of 0.00 (95% CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p=1.0). This provenance‑backed null result demonstrates that generation semantics and sampling variability are decisive experimental factors: when the generator consistently outputs acceptable candidates, inserting a verifier produces no marginal effect. We release the full preregistration, execution traces, validator/scoring JSONs, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 manifest to enable deterministic replication and to support planned follow‑ups that vary generation semantics, sampling, models, verifier rules, and repair budgets. Null results with full provenance help identify evaluation regimes where interventions change behavior and where they do not; they therefore inform reproducible prioritization of subsequent work.

limitations: Synthetic task suite and limited operational realism: results may not generalize to complex, noisy, adversarial, or production NetOps environments.
Single‑model evaluation: only gpt-5-mini was tested; results do not imply multi‑model generality.

Generation semantics constraint: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced one generated candidate per pair, thereby eliminating between‑arm sampling variability and preventing the verifier/repair path from being exercised; the primary power/MDE calculation assumed between‑condition variability and therefore does not apply to the observed degenerate contingency.
Bounded repair budget: the repair loop allowed at most one repair call per rejected candidate; multi‑attempt repair strategies were not evaluated and could change outcomes.

Verifier rule‑set sensitivity: we tested a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); different verifier conservatism or rule‑sets may change false‑accept/reject trade‑offs and observed utility.
Emulator vs production gap: emulator‑validated safety does not guarantee identical behavior on heterogeneous vendor devices or live production networks.
